Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks

SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for
Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use

Rongzhe Wei ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: Amazon Email: rongzhew@amazon.com    Ge Shi11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Amazon Email: gegshi@amazon.com    Min Cheng Affiliation: Amazon Email: mmcheng@amazon.com    Sarthak Ghosh Affiliation: Amazon Email: ghossart@amazon.com    Vaibhav Gorde Affiliation: Amazon Email: gordev@amazon.com    Leman Akoglu Affiliation: Amazon Email: lakoglu@amazon.com    Pan Li Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: panli@gatech.edu    Na Zhang Affiliation: Amazon Email: naazhang@amazon.com
Abstract

Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks—mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime—they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories. We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ∼\sim1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric—a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome—that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness.11 1 https://geshijoker.github.io/slate/

1 Introduction

Large language models have become capable tool-using agents that autonomously call external APIs to solve real-world tasks [1, 2], with growing potential to automate complex workflows across e-commerce [3, 4], software development [5], and scientific discovery [6]. Nowhere is this more consequential than inside enterprises. Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate their standard operating procedures (SOPs): given a procedure and a large library of internal software-service APIs—often hundreds to thousands—the agent should map each step to the right tool call and execute it, without engineers hand-authoring a mapping from every step to a concrete API [7, 8]. This demands agents that select and compose tools reliably over long horizons in large action spaces, precisely the setting of tool-augmented agents in e-commerce operations such as catalog, order, pricing, and customer-service management [3]. Claims of progress on such agents are only as trustworthy as the benchmarks behind them, yet existing tool-use benchmarks do not reflect this regime: small, controlled environments expose only a handful of tools [9, 10]; large tool libraries grade single-step invocation or retrieval rather than long-horizon execution [11, 12, 13]; and end-to-end evaluations typically fall back on subjective, non-reproducible LLM-as-a-judge scoring [8, 14]. What is missing is a benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise setting, where success is judged only by whether the overall task completes. We close this gap with SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a benchmark designed from the enterprise regime backward. Our contributions are:

  • •

    SLATE, a benchmark for large-scale API selection under end-to-end evaluation. SLATE is, to our knowledge, the first tool-use benchmark to jointly demand large tool spaces (∼\sim1,000 tools), long-horizon procedures, and deterministic tool outcomes, instantiated in a realistic e-commerce domain (Fig. 1). Its core is a deterministic, context-aware simulator that executes every procedure without implementing thousands of live APIs, enabling an end-to-end task-success metric: a trajectory succeeds iff it reaches every reference outcome of the task, crediting functionally equivalent solution paths while avoiding the subjectivity and false penalties of LLM-as-a-judge.

  • •

    A benchmarking study. Evaluating six open decision models and the language models they are built on (3B–12B parameters) shows SLATE is discriminative and that current models fall well short, providing an objective, reproducible yardstick for enterprise API selection.

2 The SLATE Benchmark

SLATE targets the conditions under which enterprise tool-use agents operate: selecting among a large tool library (∼\sim1,000 e-commerce APIs) to execute a long-horizon, hierarchical plan with step-wise deterministic outcomes. Each instance pairs a user query with a hierarchical solution plan whose substeps are grounded to reference tool calls, together with the simulated outputs needed to verify execution (Fig. 1). Instances are produced by a four-stage pipeline—query generation, hierarchical plan generation, tool grounding, and context-aware simulation—followed by manual quality control; we summarize construction below and give full details, including prompt templates, in Appendix A.

Existing tool-use benchmarks typically capture only part of the challenge. Small-scale settings such as τ\tau-Bench [9], AlfWorld [10], and AppWorld [15] (457 APIs across nine apps) support controlled evaluation but do not reflect large tool spaces, while benchmarks with broader tool libraries often emphasize tool retrieval or single-step correctness rather than verifiable end-to-end execution [8, 16, 13, 11, 12, 14]. Table 1 organizes prior datasets along four complementary properties: Large Tool Spaces, Long-Horizon Execution, Deterministic Tool Outcomes, and End-to-End Outcome Evaluation. SLATE is designed to satisfy all four simultaneously, enabling objective evaluation even when multiple execution trajectories reach the same correct final state.

2.1 Dataset Construction

SLATE is built by a pipeline of query collection, hierarchical plan generation, tool definition and grounding, tool simulation, and manual post-processing, so that every instance is both logically sound and executable.

Query collection. We target e-commerce because its buyer–seller workflows naturally require coordinating many interdependent APIs. Working with domain experts, we define eleven representative task categories—Pre-purchase Product Questions, Product Search & Comparison, Gifts & Discount Codes, Order & Delivery Changes, and Subscriptions & Returns for buyers, and Product Information Updates, Pricing Changes, Promotions, Fulfillment & Shipping, Inventory & Sales Analytics, and Customer Questions & Reviews for sellers. For each instance we sample a focus area within a category and use Claude to generate and then progressively complicate a query, yielding both linguistic variety and operational complexity. Fig. 2 shows the resulting distribution of library tools across functional categories.

Hierarchical plan generation. Following a top-down, human-like problem-solving paradigm, each query is recursively decomposed into high-level goals, each refined into finer-grained substeps. Crucially, plan generation is performed independently of any toolset, so the decomposition reflects the natural structure of the task rather than the names of available tools, which avoids tool-specific bias in the resulting plans.

Tool definition and grounding. For each substep that requires a tool, we define the tool in a normalized schema specifying its name, input arguments, functionality, and output format, guided by three principles. First, tools must be specific rather than trivially mirror the substep text, so that tool selection remains non-trivial. Second, because execution plans carry strong sequential dependencies, we ensure that later tools take arguments derivable from earlier outputs or from the original query. Third, to promote reuse and avoid redundancy, we embed every tool’s name and description with ModernBERT and, for each new query, retrieve the fifty most semantically related existing tools, encouraging the model to reuse them and to create new tools only when genuinely novel functionality is needed. A normalization pass then groups tools into functional categories, merges semantically equivalent ones while reconciling their input and output arguments, and updates the plans accordingly, yielding a coherent, unified plan–tool structure across the dataset.

Tool simulator. Because implementing a thousand live APIs is infeasible, SLATE approximates tool execution with a simulator composed of two modules. A context-aware simulation database stores ground-truth traces: during construction, each plan is annotated with its correct tool calls and argument dependencies, and Claude generates a coherent trace of simulated outputs conditioned on the query, the full plan, and prior input–output pairs, stored as a (tool, arguments)→\rightarrowoutcome lookup together with a default response for mismatched calls. A deterministic matcher then maps an agent’s runtime call to a stored entry beyond exact string comparison, using fixed normalization rules that absorb differences in format (e.g., date conventions) and phrasing; on a successful match it returns the recorded outcome, and otherwise the tool’s default response. Every reference solution passes the simulator. This produces realistic, reproducible feedback and lets SLATE measure end-to-end task success automatically. Prompt templates for every stage are provided in Appendix A.

2.2 Scale and Statistics

Table 2 summarizes SLATE’s scale. The benchmark pairs a curated set of complex queries with a tool library of roughly one thousand APIs, of which only a small task-relevant subset is “real” for any given instance while the remainder act as distractors that make selection realistic. Plans are hierarchical and long-horizon, so each instance requires an agent to chain many dependent tool calls whose arguments are derived from earlier outputs. This combination – broad tool space, deep plans, and balanced category coverage across the eleven task categories – is what places instances in the large-toolset, long-horizon regime that motivates the benchmark.

3 Experiments

Setup. The experiments test the task SLATE is built for: mapping each step of a human-centric procedure to the API call that executes it. At every substep the model receives the user query, the earlier substeps with their reference tools and outputs, and the current substep, and selects one of 52 candidates, one per single-character option label (A–Z, a–z), so that the option encoding is identical across models. The candidates always include the reference tool and a “no tool needed” option; the other 50 are the library tools most similar to the substep under Cohere Embed v4 [25], and all 52 are listed in a fixed shuffled order. To isolate API selection, the simulator runs a correctly selected tool with its reference arguments when the steps it depends on were also selected correctly, so one wrong selection breaks every step that depends on it. We report task success, the share of tasks that reach every reference outcome (the recorded outputs of the final step and of every step whose output no later step uses), and step-wise accuracy, the share of substeps with the correct selection, each averaged over three option orders.

Models. A decision model, also called a System-1 model after the fast, intuitive mode of dual-process theory [26], is a language model fine-tuned to answer multiple-choice questions directly: given a state, a question, and a list of options, it returns a calibrated probability for every option in a single forward pass instead of generating free-form text [27, 28, 29, 30]. We evaluate six open decision models, each paired with the backbone LLM it was trained from; the backbone LLM receives the same candidates and is read from its next-token probabilities over the option labels (Appendix B shows an example). The models span five backbone families from 3B to 12B parameters; checkpoints and prompts are listed in Appendix B.

Results. Table 3 shows that SLATE is far from solved. Even though the reference tool is always among the candidates, step-wise accuracy ranges from 36.6% to 74.8%, and per-step errors compound over the dependent substeps of a task. If each of a task’s 10.6 tool steps were selected correctly with independent probability pp, the task would succeed with probability p10.6p^{10.6}, about 4.7% for p=0.75p=0.75; the best observed task success is 5.0%. Decision models improve step-wise accuracy over their backbone LLMs in four of six pairs (by 6.6–15.7 points), whereas both Strands deciders trail their Gemma backbones (by 17.8 and 20.3 points), so decision-model training does not uniformly help on this task. Results vary little across option orders (standard deviation at most 1.3 points). SLATE is therefore far from saturated for small models, leaving substantial room for future work on reliable long-horizon API selection.

4 Conclusion

We presented SLATE, a large-scale benchmark that tests what enterprise tool-use actually demands: selecting among ∼\sim1,000 APIs over a long horizon, and being graded by a deterministic, end-to-end task-success metric that accepts any valid trajectory rather than matching a single reference trace or relying on a subjective judge. Experiments with open decision models and the language models they are built on (Section 3) show that current models still fall well short, establishing SLATE as a challenging benchmark for reliable enterprise API selection. Beyond ranking agents, SLATE is intended as a testbed for improving them: a natural next step is to study different test-time-scaling strategies that spend rollout compute where it most improves end-to-end success, toward more efficient agents for enterprise API-matching problems. We release the dataset, the context-aware simulator, and the evaluation harness so the community can measure enterprise agents objectively and reproducibly, and extend the construction pipeline to new domains. By isolating API selection at scale under realistic task-level feedback, SLATE provides a reproducible yardstick for enterprise tool-use agents and, we hope, a foundation for developing more reliable and compute-efficient ones. Limitations and ethical considerations are discussed in Appendix C.

Appendices

Appendix A SLATE Construction

A.1 Prompt Templates

A.2 An Example of SLATE Data

This section presents an illustrative example in the SLATE format, illustrating the transformation from a user query to a hierarchical execution plan, associated tool calls, and deterministic simulation outputs. The example demonstrates the procedure structure and execution semantics used for step-wise and end-to-end evaluation.

Appendix B Experimental Details

Candidates. Every candidate list contains 52 options, one per single-character label (A–Z, then a–z), which keeps the option encoding identical across models. Two options are always present: the reference tool and a “no_tool_needed” option. The other 50 are retrieved with Cohere Embed v4 (cohere.embed-v4): library tools are ranked by the cosine similarity between the embedding of “name: description” and the embedding of the user query concatenated with the substep text, and the 50 highest-ranked tools other than the reference tool are kept. The list is shuffled with a seed derived from the task and substep identifiers, and the same order is shown to a decision model and to its backbone LLM; two further orders are drawn with different seeds. Because the reference tool is always included, retrieval does not cap accuracy in these experiments. Without this guarantee, the 51 top-ranked tools would contain the reference tool for 91.1% of tool substeps, and for every tool substep of a task in only 48% of tasks.

Context. The state lists the user query and every earlier substep with its reference tool and simulated output. Each earlier output is truncated to 400 characters, so that every prompt fits in a 4,096-token window.

Scoring. The prerequisites of a substep are the earlier tool steps whose outputs its reference arguments use. A correctly selected tool counts as executed only when all of its prerequisites were executed. A task succeeds when every reference outcome is reached, i.e., the recorded outputs of the final tool step and of every tool step whose output no later step uses.

Readouts. Each decision model uses its own published inference recipe (prompt format and readout) on the shared state, step, and candidates. Each backbone LLM receives the prompt below through its chat template with thinking disabled, and its prediction is the label (A–Z, a–z) with the highest next-token probability. All checkpoints are pinned to the revisions in Table 4 and run in bf16 with Hugging Face Transformers.

Decision models versus LLMs: an example. A regular LLM answers by generating text, which must then be parsed into a choice. A decision model instead scores the given options and returns a probability distribution over them in one forward pass. To compare the two on equal terms, we read the backbone LLM’s next-token probabilities over the option labels. Figure 12 shows one logged decision from our runs.

Error analysis. Table 5 breaks errors down by type. Nearly all errors select a wrong tool; skipping a needed tool or calling a tool for a no-tool substep is rare. Accuracy on substeps whose description names the reference tool is similar to or lower than on the other substeps. Table 6 reports results by task category.

Appendix C Limitations and Ethical Considerations

Limitations. SLATE is synthetic: its queries, procedures, and tool schemas are LLM-generated and its execution outcomes come from a simulator rather than live APIs. This enables reproducible, large-scale evaluation but does not capture the full behavioral complexity of real enterprise systems. Because generation used Claude models, our study evaluates non-Claude, open models to avoid rewarding generator-family bias; a sweep over larger and closed models is left to future work. Our results cover six open models up to 12B parameters evaluated on SLATE itself—we do not report cross-benchmark or cross-domain comparisons here. They isolate API selection by supplying reference arguments to correctly selected tools; argument generation is supported by the harness but not evaluated here. Some substep descriptions name their reference tool (16.1% of tool steps), although accuracy on these substeps is not higher than on the others (Table 5). The benchmark is instantiated in e-commerce; while the construction pipeline is domain-agnostic, validating difficulty in other domains (e.g., IT operations, finance) remains future work. Finally, runtime call variations are matched to recorded entries by fixed normalization rules, which may reject some valid paraphrases of free-form argument values.

Ethical considerations. SLATE contains only synthetic data and no personally identifying information. It is released for research on evaluating and improving tool-use agents; as with any automation benchmark, deployment of agents trained or selected against it should include human oversight for consequential actions.
